title: Supervisory Stress Test Documentation Final 2026 Global Market Shock Component

source.name: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

summary: The Federal Reserve published final documentation for the 2026 Global Market Shock (GMS) component of its supervisory stress tests, describing the hypothetical market distress scenario applied to trading and counterparty credit positions at large banks. The GMS applies instantaneous shocks to risk factors including equities, currencies, commodities, interest rates, and credit spreads in Q1 of the severely adverse scenario projection horizon, with no subsequent changes. This document finalizes the October 2025 proposed version with only typographical corrections.
key_points: Firms with $50 billion or more in aggregate trading assets/liabilities, or trading assets ≥10% of total consolidated assets, must incorporate the global market shock.
The global market shock applies mark-to-market accounting per U.S. GAAP, unlike accrual accounting for traditional banking activities in macro scenarios.
Losses from the global market shock are recognized entirely in Q1 of the projection horizon, reflecting the scenario assumption that market dislocations can occur rapidly.
Risk factors include: public equity returns from advanced/developing economies, FX rates, government yields, swap rates, implied volatilities, commodity futures, and credit spreads.
The 2026 stress test as-of date differs from the macro scenario's December 31 date and changes annually; the 2025 cycle used October 11, 2024.
Stress test scenarios are explicitly not forecasts but hypothetical paths to assess capital resilience under adverse conditions.
why_it_matters: This methodology document defines the severity and breadth of market shocks that major U.S. bank holding companies must survive to demonstrate adequate capital. The GMS directly affects capital planning, risk management, and potentially market behavior as firms adjust portfolios to pass the test. It is technical infrastructure for banking supervision, not a direct market signal.
market_structure_context: The GMS methodology documents a comprehensive risk factor framework covering equities, rates, credit, FX, and commodities across developed and emerging markets. Risk factor relationships (primary → secondary → remaining) are modeled through correlations. Liquidity horizons are assigned to risk factors, affecting how quickly positions can be marked under stress. This represents a structured approach to systemic market stress calibration for supervisory purposes.
notes: This is methodological documentation for supervisory stress testing, not a policy decision or market signal. The document is technically within scope for 'market structure' insofar as it defines how systemic market shocks are calibrated for bank capital assessment.
